transcript.text: Listen to a talk in a psychology class.

Imagine you see someone drop their books and fall on a busy sidewalk. Would you stop to help? Most of us would say yes. But psychologists have found that the answer depends on who else is around. This is called the bystander effect: the more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help. In a famous experiment in the nineteen sixties, researchers asked students to talk over an intercom. During the conversation, one student seemed to have a medical emergency. When participants believed they were the only listener, most of them quickly went for help. When they believed four other people were listening, far fewer did. Why? Researchers suggest a main reason is diffusion of responsibility. Each person thinks, "Someone else will do something." Another reason is that people look at others to decide whether a situation is serious. If everyone stays calm, everyone assumes things are fine. Now, this doesn't mean people are cold-hearted. In fact, when emergencies are clear and dangerous, people often act. What it tells us is that a simple step can change the outcome: pick one person and ask directly, "You, in the blue jacket, call an ambulance."

transcript.text: Listen to a talk in an economics class.

Today we are going to talk about opportunity cost, one of the most useful ideas in economics. Opportunity cost is simple to define. It is the value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice. Let me give an example. Suppose you have a free Saturday. You can work at a part-time job and earn eighty dollars, or you can go hiking with friends. If you choose hiking, the opportunity cost is not the money you spend on snacks. It is the eighty dollars you could have earned. Notice that opportunity cost is not always about money. If you study for an exam instead of sleeping, the cost is the sleep you lose. Businesses think this way, too. A company that uses its building for a restaurant gives up the rent it could earn from a store. Economists say that every choice has a cost, even when no one asks you to pay. Understanding this idea helps us make better decisions, because it forces us to compare what we gain with what we lose. transcript.text: Listen to a talk in an earth science class.

Anyone who has spent time at the beach has seen the tides, the regular rise and fall of the sea. Today I'd like to explain what causes them. The main cause is the Moon. The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth, and because water can move freely, the ocean bulges toward the Moon. That creates a high tide on the side of the Earth facing it. Interestingly, there is also a second bulge on the opposite side of the planet. This happens because the Earth itself is pulled toward the Moon more strongly than the water on the far side is, so the water is left behind. As the Earth rotates, most coasts pass through two high tides and two low tides each day. The Sun also affects the tides, although less, because it is much farther away. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up, at new moon and full moon, their pulls combine, and we get unusually high tides called spring tides. When they form a right angle, the tides are weaker. These are called neap tides. Despite the name, spring tides have nothing to do with the season. Please remember that for the quiz on Friday.

transcript.text: Listen to a talk in a biology class.

Let's turn to a fascinating example of animal communication: the honeybee. When a worker bee finds a good source of food, say a field of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs what's known as a waggle dance. The bee moves in a figure-eight pattern, and in the middle of the figure she shakes her body from side to side. Now, this isn't random movement. The direction of the waggle run, relative to straight up on the honeycomb, tells the other bees the direction of the food in relation to the sun. And the length of the waggle tells them how far away it is: a longer waggle means a greater distance. The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch spent years studying this behavior, and in 1973 he shared a Nobel Prize for his work. What I find remarkable is how he tested his idea. He moved food sources to different places and watched whether the bees at the hive could find them using only the information in the dance. They could, which was strong evidence that the dance carries real information. Of course, some scientists were skeptical at first, and it took many more experiments to convince them. Still, I think it's one of the clearest examples we have of a small animal brain solving a complex problem.

Imagine you've bought a ticket to a concert for fifty dollars. On the night of the show, it's snowing heavily, you're tired, and you really don't want to go. Do you go anyway? Many people say yes, because they've already paid. Economists call this the sunk cost fallacy. A sunk cost is money, time, or effort that's already been spent and can't be recovered. The fallacy is letting that past spending influence a decision about the future. Think about it: the fifty dollars is gone whether you attend or stay home. The only question that matters is, will going be worth it from now on? Businesses make the same mistake. A company may have spent millions developing a product, and when early sales are poor, managers keep investing, saying, "We've come too far to quit." But the money already spent shouldn't be part of the calculation. What matters is whether future costs will be outweighed by future benefits. Now, I'm not saying it's easy. Quitting feels like admitting failure. But some of the best managers I've known are willing to say, "Let's stop here," and move their resources somewhere more useful. So the next time you're tempted to continue just because you've already invested, ask yourself that one question about the future.

Look at this painting from the early fourteen hundreds, and then at one from the twelve hundreds. What's the difference? In the older painting, figures look flat, and buildings seem to tilt in odd directions. In the newer one, the room seems to recede into the distance, like a real space. What changed was a technique called linear perspective. The basic idea is simple. In real life, parallel lines, such as the edges of a road, appear to meet at a single point on the horizon. Artists began to draw lines that way, and objects further away were made smaller. The architect Filippo Brunelleschi is usually credited with working out the geometry, and a writer named Leon Battista Alberti described the method in a book in the fourteen thirties. Now, here's what I find interesting. Perspective didn't just make paintings look more realistic. It changed how artists thought about their job. Instead of telling a story with symbols, they were now creating a window onto a believable world. Some historians even argue that it influenced early science, because both depended on careful observation and measurement. I wouldn't go quite that far, but the connection is certainly worth thinking about. For Thursday, read the chapter on Alberti and note how he explains the method.

Here's a question I ask every year: why do we have seasons? Most students say it's because the Earth is closer to the sun in summer and farther in winter. It sounds logical, but it's wrong. In fact, the Earth is closest to the sun in early January, in the middle of winter for the Northern Hemisphere. The real cause is the tilt of the Earth's axis, about twenty-three and a half degrees. Because of that tilt, during part of the year the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the sun, and sunlight hits it more directly. The rays are concentrated, and days are longer. Six months later, the hemisphere leans away, and the same amount of sunlight is spread over a larger area, so it feels cooler. Here's an easy way to see this: shine a flashlight straight down on a table, and then at an angle. The straight beam makes a small, bright circle. The angled beam makes a bigger, dimmer oval. Same flashlight, same energy, different intensity. Why is this misconception so common? Probably because it matches our everyday experience that closer to a heat source means warmer. That's why it's useful to test our assumptions, even when they seem obvious.

Imagine arriving at a train station in the eighteen-sixties and finding that its clock disagreed with the one in the next town. This was normal. Before railroads, every town set its clock by the sun, so noon happened at slightly different moments from place to place. That was fine when travel was slow. But trains changed everything. Some called the day of the change the day of two noons, because clocks in many places were set back and noon arrived twice. Still, the convenience was too great to ignore. The oceans contain about thirty-five grams of salt in every liter of water, yet rivers, which keep pouring into the sea, taste fresh. So where did the salt come from, and why doesn't the ocean get saltier each year? The salt comes mostly from rocks. Rain is slightly acidic, and as it falls on land, it slowly breaks down rocks and carries minerals, including sodium, into rivers. Over millions of years, these minerals have collected in the ocean. A smaller amount comes from underwater volcanoes and vents. Water, meanwhile, leaves the ocean through evaporation, but the salt stays behind. You might expect this to make the ocean saltier forever. Yet the salt level has remained fairly stable for a very long time. That is because salt is also removed. Some minerals combine with sediments and sink to the sea floor, and others become part of new rock. Scientists describe this as a balance, where the amount entering equals the amount leaving. A common mistake is to think the ocean is salty simply because the sea is old. Age matters, but balance matters more. This also explains why some enclosed lakes, which have no outlet, are far saltier than the ocean.

If you've ever noticed that a city feels hotter than the countryside around it, you've experienced an urban heat island. On a summer evening, a city can be several degrees warmer than nearby rural areas, and the difference is often largest after sunset. Why does this happen? First, materials like asphalt, concrete, and dark roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night. Second, cities have fewer plants and trees. Vegetation cools the air by releasing water vapor, a process called transpiration. Third, tall buildings block the wind and trap heat between them, and air conditioners, cars, and factories all add heat of their own. The consequences are more than just discomfort. Hotter nights increase energy use, worsen air pollution, and can be dangerous for elderly residents. So how can cities respond? Some are painting roofs white to reflect sunlight, while others plant trees along streets or build parks. A few even install green roofs, which are covered with vegetation. None of these solutions is perfect, but together they can lower the temperature noticeably. Please read chapter nine before our next meeting.

Imagine two groups of patients with the same headache. One group receives a real painkiller, and the other receives a sugar pill. Surprisingly, many in the second group report feeling better. This is the placebo effect, and it has puzzled researchers for decades. A placebo has no active ingredient, so why does it work? One explanation is expectation. If you believe a treatment will help, your brain may actually release natural chemicals that reduce pain. Another factor is the ritual of treatment, such as seeing a doctor and taking a pill. Researchers have even found that bigger pills, or ones with brand names, produce stronger effects. Because of the placebo effect, scientists who test new medicines must be careful. They usually compare the new drug with a placebo, and neither the patients nor the doctors know who got which. This design is called a double-blind trial. A medicine is considered effective only if it works better than the placebo. Notice that this doesn't mean the placebo effect is imaginary. Patients really do feel better. The question is whether the medicine adds something beyond that.
